name: referral-network
description: A cycle-checked referral graph in Python: reach counts, flow centrality, and a referral-bonus growth model

readme.html:
referral-network

A small Python module that keeps track of who referred whom and answers three questions about that graph: who has the largest downstream reach, who sits on the most referral paths, and how large a referral bonus must be to reach a growth target.

It is one file, referral_network.py, and uses only the standard library.

The referral graph

Every edge points from a referrer to a candidate, and a candidate has at most one referrer, so the graph is a forest of trees. ReferralNetwork.add_referral(referrer, candidate) refuses three kinds of edge with a ReferralError:

  • a self-referral;
  • a second referrer for a candidate who already has one;
  • an edge that would close a cycle: it walks up from the referrer towards its root and refuses if it meets the candidate.

So the graph is still a directed acyclic graph after every call.

Query Returns
network.direct_referrals(user) an iterator over the users user referred
network.all_referrals(user) an iterator over everyone downstream of user, in no fixed order
top_k_by_reach(network, k) the k users with the most people downstream
top_k_by_flow_centrality(network, k) the k users that lie on the most referral paths

Both rankings break ties by user name, A to Z.

Reach

A user's reach is the number of people downstream of them: their referrals, their referrals' referrals, and so on. The count is kept current as edges arrive. Adding referrer → candidate adds the candidate's own reach plus one to the referrer and to every user above it.

Flow centrality

Flow centrality counts the (source, target) pairs whose referral path passes through a user. With one referrer per user there is at most one path between any two users, so user u is on the path from s to t exactly when s is above u and t is below it:

flow(u) = ancestors(u) × descendants(u)

The module keeps an ancestor count for every user next to the reach count, so both rankings come from two stored numbers per user. For example:

    a          user   reach   ancestors   flow
    │          a        4         0         0
    b          b        3         1         3
    │          c        2         2         4   ← first by flow
    c          d        0         3         0
   ╱ ╲         e        0         3         0
  d   e
                         a is first by reach, c is first by flow

Cost

Operation Cost
add_referral the depth of the referrer (cycle check, reach update) plus the size of the candidate's subtree (ancestor counts)
first top_k_* call after a change one sort of all users, O(n log n); kept until the next add_referral
later top_k_* calls a slice of the sorted list, O(k)

Growth model

Two functions model how a referral programme grows.

expected_network_size(p, days) starts with 100 referrers. Each referrer can make at most 10 successful referrals and succeeds on a given day with probability p. Everyone referred joins the next day as a new referrer with all 10. The function tracks the expected number of referrers at each remaining capacity, day by day from day 0 to day days, and returns 100 plus the expected number of referrals.

min_bonus_for_target(days, target_network_size, adoption_prob) finds the smallest bonus, in steps of $10, whose adoption probability adoption_prob(bonus) lifts the expected network size to the target, assuming a larger bonus never lowers the probability. It doubles the bonus from $10 until the target is met, then searches below that bound by bisection. It returns 0 when no bonus is needed, and None when the target is out of reach: the probability gets to 1 and the target is still not met, or the probability stops changing for five doublings in a row. Each bonus is passed to adoption_prob at most once, because that call may be expensive.

Usage

Python 3.9 or newer (the module uses built-in generic types such as list[str]).

from referral_network import (
    ReferralNetwork,
    expected_network_size,
    top_k_by_flow_centrality,
    top_k_by_reach,
)

network = ReferralNetwork()
for referrer, candidate in [("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "d"), ("c", "e")]:
    network.add_referral(referrer, candidate)

top_k_by_reach(network, 2)            # ['a', 'b']
top_k_by_flow_centrality(network, 2)  # ['c', 'b']
expected_network_size(0.5, 1)         # 225.0
network.add_referral("e", "a")        # ReferralError: Adding this referral would create a cycle

Tests

python3 -m pip install pytest
python3 -m pytest

The tests in test_referral_network.py cover the three refusals, both rankings (including a graph built bottom-up, where a referrer is attached above an existing subtree), cache refresh after a new referral, hand-computed growth values, and the three outcomes of the bonus search.
